text:
Okay, thanks. I found Q3 fairly straightforward, though thinking about *how* data would be secured was a constant undercurrent for me – it felt assumed, but crucial. The questions around fairness (Q5 and the second part of Q3) were most important; ensuring equity has to be central. 

I was surprised everyone seemed so willing to accept even a small improvement with course performance data – I think that’s fairly invasive already. And I strongly feel age, gender, race/ethnicity shouldn't *ever* be included. My own experience dropping out initially made me prioritize understanding *why* students struggle; hence my strong preference for explainability, even at the cost of some accuracy. Maybe an opt-out mechanism could address data privacy concerns?

Thanks. I agree with S8 about the assumed security – that needs explicit discussion. I found Q3.5 quite difficult; distinguishing between needing a small improvement and being acceptable regardless felt…artificial. It forced me to weigh benefits too precisely when it's more nuanced than that.

For me, Q4 was most important. As an advisor, I *need* to understand why the model flagged someone – it informs how I approach the conversation. The strong consensus on prioritizing explainability is reassuring. 

I landed slightly differently on nationality and disability; a “small” improvement felt acceptable if it demonstrably helped vulnerable students, but only with very robust safeguards. I'm surprised so many chose 'never'. Perhaps they’re more attuned to systemic biases within those data points than I am? That opt-out is a good idea – vital, even.

Thanks both of you. I agree with A1 about Q3.5 feeling artificial - it’s hard to put a number on improving identification when we're talking about people’s lives. For me, those questions were all about risk versus reward, and the risks around sensitive data felt too high for even small gains. As an international student who also works part-time, I’m already aware of being potentially categorised differently.

I think Q4 – explainability – is the most crucial. It’s not enough to just *know* someone might be struggling; we need to understand *why*, so support can be tailored and appropriate. I was glad to see strong agreement there, though surprised at how many were okay with moderate explainability at a cost of accuracy. The opt-out is essential – control over my own data feels vital, especially as a non-EU national.

Thanks everyone. I agree with A1 about Q3.5 feeling forced – quantifying improvement felt…reductionist when we're talking about student wellbeing. As an advisor, I’m used to looking at the whole picture, and these questions made me think too much about isolated data points.

I found Q4 the most critical; explainability is non-negotiable for me. I *have* to be able to justify reaching out to a student based on more than just an algorithm saying so. The strong preference for high explainability aligns with my practice. 

I was slightly surprised by the ‘never’ responses on nationality and disability – while completely understanding the concerns about bias, as someone working directly with students, I worry about missing those who *need* help most if we exclude potentially useful data entirely. Perhaps tiered access or stricter auditing of that data could be a compromise?

Thanks everyone. I found Q3.5 really difficult too – trying to quantify ‘improvement’ felt wrong when it's about student wellbeing. It feels like we’re prioritizing metrics over people a bit.

I think the explainability questions (Q4) are *hugely* important, especially because of my own experiences with ADHD and navigating support systems. I need to understand *why* the model flagged me – or wouldn't - otherwise it’s useless. 

I answered ‘small’ for disability data, which seems lower than most here, but that’s because I know how easily conditions like mine can be misinterpreted. I worry about being unfairly targeted, even with good intentions. The opt-out is essential, and maybe tiered access as A3 suggested would help address the risks.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3.5 really hard – putting a number on ‘improvement’ feels…wrong when it impacts someone's support. As a student with dyslexia who's returned to education, I worry about being labelled or pre-judged by the system.

Q4, explainability, is most important for me. Knowing *why* I was flagged would be vital – especially because of my learning difference; is it genuinely struggle, or something the model misinterprets? 

I answered “small” for disability data, and that felt a tough call. It’s useful to identify students who might need extra help, but I’m wary of being singled out. The opt-out is essential, and tiered access – maybe advisors seeing more detail than the system initially reveals – could be helpful.

Thanks everyone. I agree with A1 and S2 about Q3.5 feeling artificial; assigning numbers to ‘improvement’ when it's about wellbeing feels…off. As someone managing a chronic health condition *while* studying, I found those questions particularly stressful – what constitutes 'improvement' for me might be different than for others. 

Q4, explainability, is absolutely critical. Having used disability support services, I know how important understanding the ‘why’ is. If flagged, knowing *what* triggered it allows me to address it proactively and advocate for myself. I strongly support the opt-out mechanism – control over my data feels essential, especially given my health history. The tiered access idea from A3 & S7 also sounds promising.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – Q3.5 felt really difficult and artificial. Trying to put a number on ‘improvement’ when we're talking about someone’s wellbeing feels…wrong. My own experience dropping out, and being an EU national learning Danish, makes me particularly sensitive to being categorized.

For me, explainability (Q4) is *hugely* important too – I need to understand why a model might flag me. Given my past dropout, that could easily be misinterpreted. I answered 'small' for nationality and first-gen status because those factors can genuinely impact access to support, but only with really careful safeguards. The opt-out mechanism is essential, and tiered access, as A3 & S7 suggested, seems like a good compromise.

Thanks everyone. I agree with many points already raised – Q3.5 *did* feel artificial, trying to quantify benefit when we’re dealing with individual students. As an advisor for eleven years, I'm used to holistic assessment; these isolated data points felt…limited.

For me, the explainability questions (Q4) are paramount. If a model flags a student, I *need* to understand why to have a productive conversation and offer appropriate support. A ‘black box’ is useless in my role. 

I answered “moderate” on most of the data additions in Q3 – a small improvement justifies the privacy trade-off if it truly helps more vulnerable students. While I strongly support an opt-out, I'm worried about exacerbating existing inequalities if we exclude potentially useful data entirely. Perhaps regular audits of model fairness are key?

Thanks everyone. I found Q3.5 really difficult too – trying to decide what level of ‘improvement’ was worth a privacy trade-off felt…icky. As someone who dropped out and came back, I'm *very* aware of being labelled.

Q4 - explainability - is massively important for me. Knowing why the model flagged me would be vital; did it see my late submissions because of work, or something else? A lack of understanding feels scary. 

I answered 'small’ for first-gen/financial aid data because those experiences *do* impact access to support, but I worry about being pre-judged. The opt-out is essential, and this tiered access idea sounds promising – let advisors see more detail to provide better context.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said - Q3.5 *did* feel artificial. Trying to put a number on ‘improvement’ when it concerns someone's wellbeing is… unsettling. Being an international student, still adjusting, makes me particularly cautious about data privacy – it feels like extra scrutiny.

For me, explainability (Q4) is crucial. As I’m new to the Danish system, understanding *why* a model flagged me would be vital; is it my performance, or something related to how I learn? I answered 'small' for nationality and first-gen status - those factors can influence support needs – but with safeguards. The opt-out is essential, and tiered access seems like a good balance between privacy and support.

Thanks everyone. I agree with so much that’s been said, especially about Q3.5 feeling artificial – quantifying ‘improvement’ when it's about wellbeing *does* feel wrong. As a final-year Masters student managing a long-term mental health condition, the idea of being categorized by an algorithm is… unsettling. 

Q4, explainability, is vital for me. Understanding *why* I was flagged – or not – would be crucial given my fluctuating study pace. It’s about understanding if it's genuinely academic struggle or linked to my condition. I answered “small” for nationality and disability data, but with huge caveats; the opt-out is essential, and tiered access as suggested by A3 & S7 sounds very promising – advisors need context.
